Messages.Author: XZealot
Messages.Body:
Withdrawal Deals are defined as getting another player's help in
return for letting that player withdraw from the game in the two
player game when you are the only two players left.

Under the new V:EKN rules Play to Win is Defined as

4.8. Play to Win
....

Exception: when only two Methuselahs remain, the tournament rules no
longer acknowledge any deals. ***Prior deals are voided, even if they
were
play to win when made. When only two Methuselahs remain, both
Methuselahs must play to win based only on game state, without regard
to any deals.***

Wouldn't Withdrawal Deals be prohibited as they can never be honored
under the tournament rules, and encourage an attempt at illegal play?

Comments Welcome,
Norman S. Brown, Jr
XZealot
Archon of the Swamp

The deal can be made and honored if it is PTW; honored, at least, until two
players remain. When only two players remain, then the deal is gone. The deal
doesn't exist when there are two players, so it cannot be honored nor broken.

If the players at that point can both play to win while one of them withdraws,
then that's PTW and the question of honoring some deal doesn't come up.

If withdrawing or allowing a withdrawal is not play to win, then it isn't legal,
and the question of honoring some non-existent deal doesn't change that.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <f69b4b4e-eff1-4fea...@r60g2000hsc.googlegroup


That could happen, and whoever is making the judgement call (a judge or,
in casual play, the players at the table) could bear that in mind.

Players aren't required to play for incredibly unlikely scenarios
(unless all other scenarios lead to zero). Similarly, a player who has
an infinitesimal (but non-zero) chance of a Game Win may well be playing
reasonably to aim for a very solid chance of 2VP instead.

The thing here is: ignore withdrawal. If a player makes a VP split deal
that you think is shady (for whatever reason), how do you adjudicate
that? Do the players not in the deal adjudicate? Does the whole table
adjudicate? Do you let a "senior" player adjudicate? However you
resolve every other rules or deal dispute, do the same here.

--
James Coupe

I'm talking about "dispute" as in "argument", where two people disagree
over whether something is a good deal or not. One person says "I can't
possibly get a game win on this table, it would take an asteroid
dropping on your head to let me win" and another person disagrees. Who
chooses which one is right? In a tournament, a judge. In a casual
game? However you handle such things in casual games.

>It's like saying that it's not really cheating
>unless you get caught.

It's a fairly simple fact of life that if no-one spots the cheating, it
doesn't get corrected. V:TES is no different to any other game in this
respect.

>How can a deal be offered and accepted that isn't legal to be
>fulfilled?

Two players may not realise that it's a poor deal, or may overlook the
fact that all deals are off at 2 players, or similar. Bottom line:
people make mistakes.

Because people make mistakes, and because you must undoubtedly deal with
mistakes anyway, extend your mistake resolution system to cope. At the
simplest level, deals which aren't legal are just non-sensical table-
talk. Point out there's no deal, correct game state (if appropriate),
and move on.

In a tournament, if a deal sounds weird, call a judge over early on so
that they can be aware of the situation when the deal was made (and can
intervene whenever is appropriate). This isn't necessary, it can just
make everyone's life simpler.

Out of interest, is there a reason for your tendency to spot a random
word in a follow-up, and then make wildly different points that are only
slightly relevant to the points made in the previous post?



This for That (or something for something) is the basis for all

How can you put a rule in the VEKN rules that is unenforceable in the
most blatant of situation?

4.8. Play to Win
....

Exception: when only two Methuselahs remain, the tournament rules no

longer acknowledge any deals. ***Prior deals are voided, even if they
were
play to win when made. When only two Methuselahs remain, both
Methuselahs must play to win based only on game state, without regard
to any deals.***

How can it be legal for a deal to be made that will affect the balance
of a table that will be voided and never fulfilled, but yet you know
that you will have players, who "never break a deal, ever, ever, ever"
that will attempt to subvert the above rule whilst attempting to
uphold the deal.

This put judges in the tenuous position of trying to judge whether the
players behavior is in violation of the above rule or just bad play,
when it is just easier for the judges to void a deal when it is
offered rather than 3 turns later.

An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

You're mistaking "not illegal" for "uneforceable".

The rule is enforceable.

The deal in question is legal.

The activity in question is legal (being play to win), both while the deal is in
effect and after it no longer exists.

Playing to win does not violate the play to win rule.
